title: How Should the Church Relate to the State? Five Views
subtitle: Five traditions on how the people of God relate to the governing power — two kingdoms, transformation, witness, the two cities, and theonomy — for the believer trying to hold faith and citizenship at once.
triageNote: That Christ is Lord, that his people owe the state honor and real obedience within its limits, and that no earthly power may claim the worship due to God alone — this is shared ground across the faithful. How the church and the state are meant to relate, whether Christians should hold power and reform culture or witness from the margins, is where the traditions part. This is second-order. It is not the creedal floor; the Nicene faith does not bind you to Kuyper or to Hauerwas. Faithful churches, reading the same Scripture, have landed across this whole range, and they remain churches to one another. Hold your position with conviction and your brother across the aisle with honor.
question: What is the relationship between the church and the state, between the people of God and the governing power under which they live? Political theology is the branch of Christian thought that asks it: how the two kingdoms, or the two cities, fit together; whether the believer's task is to reform the public order under Christ's lordship or to witness to it as an alternative community; what obedience the state may rightly command and where that obedience must stop. You cannot settle it with a single verse, because Scripture holds Romans 13, which calls the ruler God's servant, in the same canon as Revelation 13, which unveils the ruler as a beast. The whole tradition is an attempt to hold both.
whyItMatters:
This is the question the American church has answered worst in living memory, and I include myself in the failure. We have watched the gospel get strapped to a party until, for millions who will never darken a church door, the word Christian now names a voting bloc before it names anything about Christ. That is not the fault of the unbeliever who assumes it. It is our fault, for handing them the impression.

Every believer answers this question, whether they know it or not. The one who says faith and politics do not mix has taken a position, a version of the two-kingdoms view, as surely as the one who storms a capital with a cross on a flag. There is no neutral seat. How you relate the church to the state shapes how you vote, whether you can love an enemy across an aisle, what you expect from a president, and whether your hope finally rests in an election or somewhere an election cannot reach.

And the stakes are not only personal. The church's witness to the watching world hangs on this. When we confuse the kingdom of God with an earthly power, we do not make the power holy; we make the gospel sound like a lie in the mouths of the people who most needed to hear it. When we abandon the public square entirely, we can leave the vulnerable undefended and call our absence faithfulness. Both are ways of losing. This entry maps the roads the church has taken between them, not to tell you which to walk, but so that you walk it with your eyes open.

positions.name: The Two Kingdoms
positions.inOneLine: God rules the world two ways at once, the spiritual kingdom through the gospel and the church, the temporal kingdom through the magistrate and the sword, and the Christian lives faithfully in both without collapsing either into the other.
positions.bestCase:
Begin with a distinction Martin Luther drew in the years after 1520 and the Reformed confessions kept. God governs his world through two kingdoms, or two governments. In the spiritual kingdom he rules through the word, the gospel, the forgiveness of sins, and the church; his instrument is preaching, and his aim is faith. In the temporal kingdom he rules through law, the magistrate, and yes the sword; his instrument is coercion, and his aim is a measure of order and justice among sinners who would otherwise devour one another. Both are God's. Neither is the devil's realm. But they run by different rules, and the peace of the world depends on not confusing them.

The magistrate does not preach, and the preacher does not carry the sword. When Paul says the governing authorities are instituted by God and bear the sword to punish evil, he is describing a pagan Rome, not a baptized one. The state does not need to be Christian to be legitimate; it needs to be just. That is why a believer can serve as a soldier or a judge in good conscience, and why the gospel advances by testimony and never by the magistrate's compulsion. Faith cannot be commanded by law.

David VanDrunen has recovered this for our own day. The civil kingdom is common, shared with unbelievers, governed by what God has written on the conscience of all rather than by the distinctive ethics of the redeemed. The church as church has no mandate to run the state or to bless a party. Its citizens obey the law, pay the tax, honor the ruler, and render to Caesar what is Caesar's, while rendering to God the worship Caesar may never claim.
advocates: Martin Luther, Temporal Authority: To What Extent It Should Be Obeyed (1523)
the Lutheran and classical Reformed confessions
David VanDrunen, Living in God's Two Kingdoms

positions.name: Reformed Transformationalism and Neo-Calvinism
positions.inOneLine: There is no neutral zone and no sphere sealed off from Christ; because he is Lord over every part of life, Christians are called to bring his renewing claim to bear on culture, work, and the state alike.
positions.bestCase:
We reject the idea that faith is a private kingdom and politics a common one where Christ makes no claim. Abraham Kuyper, the Dutch theologian who became prime minister in 1901, put it in words we have never improved on. In his address opening the Free University of Amsterdam in 1880 he declared that there is not one square inch in the whole domain of human existence over which Christ, who is Sovereign over all, does not cry, Mine. If that is true, there is no square inch of politics he does not claim either.

This does not mean the church runs the state. Kuyper taught sphere sovereignty. The family, the school, the business, the church, and the government each have their own God-given authority, and none may swallow the others. The state is not the church and must not pretend to be. But every sphere, the state included, stands under the lordship of Christ and answers to him for justice.

So we do not retreat. Psalm 2 summons the kings of the earth to serve the Lord; Colossians tells us that all things were created through Christ and for him, and that in him all things hold together and are being reconciled. Culture is not a lost country to flee but a field to cultivate. The abolition of the slave trade, the fall of apartheid, the long labor for the vulnerable, were not won by Christians who kept their heads down. Tim Keller argued that the gospel makes us the best possible citizens precisely because our final hope lies elsewhere. We work for the city's good, expecting no utopia, refusing no responsibility, because the King who owns every square inch has not resigned from any of them.
advocates: Abraham Kuyper, Lectures on Calvinism and the doctrine of sphere sovereignty

positions.name: The Anabaptist and Witness Tradition
positions.inOneLine: The church's first political task is to be the church, an alternative community whose shared life under the Sermon on the Mount is itself a witness, rather than to seize the levers of a state it was never commissioned to run.
positions.bestCase:
Ask the wrong question and you will get a wrong answer for centuries. The question is not how Christians should run the government. The question is what kind of community God has called into being, and what its very existence says to the powers. Stanley Hauerwas and William Willimon, in Resident Aliens in 1989, called the church a colony, a beachhead of a new world in the middle of the old. As Hauerwas put it, the church does not have a social ethic; the church is a social ethic.

We take the Sermon on the Mount as political teaching, not private counsel. Jesus tells his people to love enemies, to refuse the sword, to forgive, to make peace, and he means it for the community that bears his name. When he stood before Pilate he said his kingdom is not of this world, and then proved it by refusing the one weapon every worldly kingdom finally trusts. Peter calls us sojourners and exiles, and exiles do not run the empire; they live faithfully inside it and let their common life indict its cruelties.

An earlier and gifted theologian of this stream, John Howard Yoder, wrote The Politics of Jesus; his personal conduct toward women was gravely and abusively wrong, a matter of public record his own church has since named, and we do not hide it. The witness rests on the community, not the man. The claim stands on its own. A church that mirrors the nation's anger, its idolatries, and its lust for power has nothing to say to the nation. A church that is genuinely an alternative has everything to say, simply by being what it is.
advocates: Stanley Hauerwas and William Willimon, Resident Aliens (1989)
the historic Anabaptist and Mennonite peace churches
the Sermon on the Mount tradition of Christian nonviolence

positions.name: The Augustinian Two Cities and Catholic Subsidiarity
positions.inOneLine: Two cities, built by two loves, run intermixed through history until God sorts them at the end; the earthly state is real and good in its limited work, but penultimate, and Christians pursue the common good within it without mistaking it for the kingdom.
positions.bestCase:
Augustine wrote The City of God between 413 and 426, after Rome was sacked, when Christians were tempted either to despair for the empire or to baptize it. He refused both. There are two cities, he said, made by two loves: the earthly city by the love of self reaching to contempt of God, the heavenly city by the love of God reaching to contempt of self. They are not two institutions you can point to on a map. They run mixed together through all of history, wheat and weeds in the same field, and only the last judgment will separate them.

This gives the state its due and its limit at once. Earthly peace is a real good; the Christian uses it, prays for it, and works for it, the way a traveler uses an inn without mistaking it for home. But no empire is the kingdom of God, and no politics will heal what only grace can heal. The state is penultimate. It keeps a rough justice among loves that are disordered.

The Catholic tradition built on this. From Leo the Thirteenth's encyclical Rerum Novarum in 1891, the founding text of modern Catholic social teaching, two principles matured: the common good, the conditions that let every person flourish, and subsidiarity, named in 1931, the rule that a higher body should never absorb what a smaller one can do for itself. The family, the parish, the union, the town each have their integrity, and the state serves them best by strengthening them, not replacing them. Politics matters enormously and saves no one. Both halves of that sentence belong to the tradition.
advocates: Catholic social teaching, from Leo XIII's Rerum Novarum (1891)
the principles of subsidiarity and the common good

positions.name: Theonomy and Christian Reconstruction
positions.inOneLine: Because God's revealed law is the perfect standard of justice and does not expire, the civil magistrate remains obligated to govern by it, including the case laws and sanctions God gave Israel, rather than by an autonomous reason that answers to no king.
positions.bestCase:
Every legal order enforces someone's morality; the only question is whose. The secular state pretends to neutrality while smuggling in its own ultimate commitments. We say the choice is not between God's law and no law, but between God's law and the law of some other god. R. J. Rushdoony, in his Institutes of Biblical Law in 1973, pressed the point that abandoning the law of God does not free a society; it merely hands the throne to the autonomous human will.

Our argument is one of continuity. God gave Israel not only worship but a whole civil order, and he called the surrounding nations to marvel at its justice: what great nation, Moses asks, has statutes so righteous as this whole law. Jesus said he came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it, and that not a stroke would pass from it. The moral substance of God's law, including the equity of its civil penalties, reveals what justice actually is. Why would the God who defines justice leave the magistrate to guess at it?

So we hold that the civil ruler is a servant of God, as Paul says in Romans 13, and a servant is not free to invent his own standard. Isaiah calls the Lord our judge, our lawgiver, our king. A nation is blessed when its laws conform to his and cursed when they defy him. We do not seek to impose faith, which cannot be coerced. We seek a public justice that answers to the God who is really there, rather than to the shifting will of the majority, which is only tyranny with better manners.
advocates: R. J. Rushdoony, The Institutes of Biblical Law (1973)
Greg Bahnsen, Theonomy in Christian Ethics

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The two-kingdoms and Augustinian readings, though every view must reckon with it
biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul commands submission to the governing authorities, who are instituted by God and bear the sword as God's servant to punish wrongdoing and reward good; so pay taxes, revenue, respect, and honor. He wrote it under Nero, not a Christian prince.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for the Anabaptist and pacifist stream, since the authority God appoints bears the sword. And hard for theonomy, since Paul commends submission to a pagan Rome without ever telling it to adopt the law of Moses.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The two-kingdoms reader sees a legitimate secular authority that need not be Christian to be just. The Anabaptist notes the passage tells the church to submit, not to wield, and reads it alongside Revelation 13. The transformationalist hears the ruler named God's servant and therefore accountable to God's justice. The theonomist presses that same phrase, servant of God, to mean the ruler owes his obedience to God's revealed standard.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Standing before Pilate, Jesus says his kingdom is not of this world; if it were, his servants would fight to prevent his arrest. The King declines the sword at the one moment a worldly king would seize it.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any triumphalism, whether theonomic or transformational, that expects Christ's kingdom to be established by holding coercive power, since the King himself refuses that power at the decisive hour.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The two-kingdoms reader hears that the spiritual kingdom does not advance by compulsion. The Anabaptist hears that the refusal of the sword is the very shape of the kingdom. The Kuyperian answers that not of this world names the kingdom's source and character, not its absence from this world, since the same Christ claims every square inch; the phrase is about origin, not location.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The two-kingdoms and Augustinian readings, and a rebuke to totalizing claims of every kind
biblicalEvidence.summary: Handed a coin that bears Caesar's image, Jesus says render to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's. Matthew 22:21 records the same saying. Caesar gets his coin; God gets what bears his image, the human being.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for theonomy, which resists a legitimate secular sphere with its own coin, and hard for any nationalism that hands Caesar the allegiance that belongs to God.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The two-kingdoms reader finds two distinct claims, neither of them absolute. The Augustinian sees the state given a real but penultimate due. The transformationalist argues that even Caesar's sphere is under God, so the saying limits Caesar rather than dividing the world in half. The Anabaptist hears an invitation to hand the empire back its idols and belong wholly to God.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Jeremiah writes to the exiles in Babylon: seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you, and pray to the Lord on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare. Live and build and bless, even here.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for a withdrawn separatism that would let the pagan city rot, and equally hard for a triumphalism that would seize the city rather than seek its good as a resident guest.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The exile reading hears a people who are resident aliens, blessing the city without ruling it. The transformationalist hears a mandate for full civic engagement and cultural labor. The two-kingdoms reader hears that the welfare sought is a common, this-worldly good, not the planting of the church by the state. All agree Babylon is not home.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The Anabaptist and critical readings, the necessary counterweight to Romans 13
biblicalEvidence.summary: John sees a beast rising from the sea, given its authority by the dragon, making war on the saints and demanding worship. It is the state absolutized into an idol that persecutes those who will not bow.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view that reads Romans 13 alone and hears only obey; the same canon that calls the state God's servant also unveils it as a worship-demanding beast. Hard, too, for a transformationalism that grows comfortable with power.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Anabaptist sees what the state becomes when it forgets it is penultimate, so the church's non-conformity is faithfulness. The two-kingdoms reader says the magistrate that demands worship has left its lane and forfeits the obedience Romans 13 asks. The Augustinian sees the earthly city, loving self to the contempt of God, showing its true face. All agree there is a line past which submission becomes idolatry, as the apostles said, we must obey God rather than men.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Be subject to every human institution, to the emperor and his governors, for the Lord's sake; live as free, yet as servants of God. Then the careful ranking: honor everyone, love the brotherhood, fear God, honor the emperor.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for a revolutionary theonomy or a politics of seizing power, since Peter counsels honor and subjection under a hostile Nero. And hard for total withdrawal, since he commands honor and engagement, not retreat.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Every tradition notices the order Peter sets: fear God, honor the emperor, and never the reverse. The two-kingdoms reader honors the office without absolutizing it. The Anabaptist reads free servants of God who submit as exiles. The emperor is given honor; God alone is given fear.

biblicalEvidence.summary: The nations rage and the kings of the earth take counsel against the Lord and his Anointed. God installs his King on Zion and summons the rulers of the earth to serve the Lord with fear and to kiss the Son.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for a two-kingdoms view that would seal politics off from Christ's direct lordship, since the psalm places the kings of the earth under explicit obligation to the Son.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Kuyperian hears that the risen Christ reigns now over the nations, so no ruler is autonomous. The two-kingdoms reader answers that the psalm is fulfilled in Christ's spiritual reign, pressed home through the gospel, not in a program to Christianize the state by law. The Anabaptist hears a King who rules from a cross as well as a throne, summoning the nations by witness rather than conquest. All confess Christ is Lord of the rulers, and divide on what that requires of the ruler now.

weighing:
Let me tell you where I land, and name it as one pastor's judgment inside a family argument, not the verdict of the whole church. Take it as a considered opinion, offered without contempt for the brothers who land elsewhere.

I read the Bible as giving us Babylon before it gives us Jerusalem restored. The people of God spend most of Scripture as exiles, sojourners, a minority under someone else's flag, told to seek the city's welfare and to keep from bowing to its idols. And I think the long age of Christendom, when the church held the sword and wrote the law, is over in the West, and that its ending is not only a loss to mourn but a clarity to receive. We are back where the New Testament first found us. That pushes me toward the Augustinian and the Anabaptist witness held together: the church's first political act is to be the church, an alternative community whose common life is itself a testimony, seeking the good of the neighbor and the city without mistaking any party or nation for the kingdom, and without expecting the magistrate to do the church's work.

But I will not pretend the strongest objection does not land. The Kuyperian and the transformationalist ask the question I cannot fully answer. If the faithful withdraw from power in the name of witness, who is left to defend the vulnerable at the gate? William Wilberforce did not end the slave trade by tending a contrast community; he worked the levers of a wicked Parliament for twenty years. The civil-rights movement was the Black church seizing a public moment, not retreating from it. Withdrawal can be obedience. It can also become a comfortable name for abandoning the neighbor to injustice while we keep our own hands clean. I feel the weight of that, and I have not escaped it.

Seek the welfare of the city. The command does not tell us exactly how close to the fire to stand, and faithful believers, reading the same book, will stand at different distances. I hold my position and I keep the argument open, because the neighbor's suffering will not wait for us to finish it.
charitableDisagreement:
If you are a Kuyperian, hear me say it plainly. You are not a power-worshiper for believing Christ claims the ballot box and the statehouse. You are trying to obey a Lord who really does own every square inch, and you have the abolitionists and the reformers at your side, Christians who loved their neighbors enough to change the law. When you engage, you are not selling out; you are stewarding an authority you believe your King delegated. I take that seriously, and the church needs you, because the alternative to your engagement is too often a congregation that lets the world burn and calls its silence purity.

And if you are a Hauerwasian, hear the same respect. You are not a quietist hiding from responsibility. You are guarding something the activists keep forgetting, that the church's first gift to the world is to be a community the world could not have produced on its own, and that a church which grabs for power usually ends by baptizing the power and losing the church. You have watched the gospel get harnessed to a party and shrink into a mascot, and your refusal is not cowardice but memory.

You share more than divides you, and it weighs more. Neither of you will give Caesar what belongs to God. One of you seeks the city's welfare from inside its institutions; the other seeks it by being a city within the city. You are arguing about the road, not the destination, and you will need each other on it, the engaged Christian to keep the witness from curdling into a hiding place, the witnessing Christian to keep the engagement from hardening into an idol. Sit at the same table. You are closer than the noise between you suggests.

relatedDebates.topic: Christian nationalism and where allegiance becomes idolatry
relatedDebates.note: Every tradition here draws a line between honoring a nation and worshiping it, but they draw it in different places. When does patriotism, a fitting love for one's own people, curdle into the claim that a particular nation is God's chosen instrument and its enemies God's enemies? The two-kingdoms and Anabaptist voices tend to see the danger earliest; the transformationalist worries that calling every public conviction nationalism would shame ordinary Christians out of loving their neighbors through law. The test the whole tradition shares: the moment the cross is conscripted to bless a flag, it has become idolatry, not politics.

relatedDebates.topic: The sword, just war, and Christian pacifism
relatedDebates.note: If the state legitimately bears the sword, may the Christian wield it? The Anabaptist tradition answers no, reading the Sermon on the Mount as binding on the disciple. The Augustinian tradition developed the just-war criteria, the conditions under which force can be a grievous mercy that restrains a greater evil. Luther's two kingdoms let a believer serve as a soldier in the temporal realm while living by the gospel in the spiritual one. This debate runs straight through the church-and-state question, because what you think the sword is for decides much of what you think the state is for.

relatedDebates.topic: Religious liberty and the establishment of religion
relatedDebates.note: Should the state privilege the true faith, or guarantee a free and level ground for all? For most of Christendom the answer was establishment. The Baptist and free-church tradition, from figures like Roger Williams who founded Rhode Island in 1636, argued instead that coerced religion is no religion and that a soul cannot be compelled, which made them early and unlikely champions of liberty for everyone, unbelievers included. The theonomist resists a genuinely neutral state; the two-kingdoms thinker tends to defend it. Where you land shapes what you want the First Amendment to mean.

relatedDebates.topic: Natural law and what unbelievers can know of justice
relatedDebates.note: Can a society that does not share the faith still know real justice? The classical and Catholic traditions say yes, through natural law, a moral order written on the conscience that Paul names in Romans 2, so that Christians can make public arguments an unbeliever is able to hear. The theonomist is skeptical that fallen reason reads that law rightly and wants the written law of God instead. This quiet disagreement decides whether Christian political speech sounds like thus says the Lord or like an appeal to goods every neighbor can already recognize.
